commit.message:
Document the hardening pass and point the submission at the live product

The submission never mentioned the deployed app, the video, or any URL beyond
the repository, and omitted the frontend from the table of what was built. A
judge who did not clone and run two hardhat scripts saw no product at all.

The hardening section is the interesting half: finding and fixing a demonstrated
leak in your own privacy claim is better evidence of engineering than a feature
list, and publishing it is the honest thing to do regardless.

Also tightens the front-running write-up. The AMM half of frontrun.js is a
constant-product model evaluated locally, not a deployed pool, and it was sitting
under a heading that read as covering both halves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Show a trader the orders they sent and how each one settled

After submitting, a trader's own order vanished from the interface completely:
OrderSubmitted was declared in the ABI and queried nowhere, and Batches showed a
global feed rather than anything belonging to you.

Both events index `trader`, so the node does the filtering rather than the
browser. The one-hour search window is stated on screen rather than hidden — a
silently truncated history reads as "you have no orders", which is the wrong
thing to tell someone about their own money.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Lead the landing page with a live proof instead of a claim

Most people arriving here have never heard of front-running and have no reason
to believe a stranger's security claims. So the page now hands them a real order
off the live book and a button: the counter climbs to 250 and the number of
orders they could read stays at zero.

Beside it, the length channel we got wrong first, queried from both the
superseded book and this one. Being handed a real encrypted order and failing to
read it is a different kind of persuasion than a paragraph, and admitting the
version we shipped broken is more convincing than only ever showing the version
that works.

The app's Attack screen keeps the developer-facing version. Both share one set
of hooks so the landing and the app cannot drift into disagreeing about the
evidence.

Also corrects two pieces of copy the protocol change had made false: step five
still described claiming a fill, and the guarantees table still described the
image digest as merely checked rather than pinned.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add an Attack screen so the privacy claim can be tested, not just read

The most persuasive artifact this project had was a hardhat script, which meant
only someone who cloned the repo ever saw it.

It pulls a real order off the book and offers 250 decryption attempts against
it, which fail because the key exists only inside the TEE. Attempts run a few
per animation frame — a straight loop of 250 secp256k1 point multiplies locks
the tab, and watching the counter climb is more convincing than a number that
appears all at once anyway.

Beside it, the length channel that was genuinely broken: the superseded book and
the current one queried side by side, 157 and 158 bytes then, 353 and 353 now.
Both contracts are still on-chain and always will be, so this is evidence a
visitor can check rather than a claim they have to accept.

Showing our own broken version next to the fix is deliberate. A privacy product
that only ever shows the working case is asking to be taken on trust, which is
the one thing this project keeps arguing against.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Give deposits a way back out, and stop the tab bar overflowing on phones

Withdraw was in the ABI with no call site anywhere in the app, so deposits were
one-way through the UI. That is worst for the base asset: the app's own copy
explains FXRP is the real Coston2 FAsset and is not faucetable, so any a visitor
deposited was stranded permanently.

The form explains itself when withdrawal is blocked rather than letting the
wallet surface a raw StillExposed revert — a trader with an unresolved batch
would otherwise see a failure with no reason attached.

The app tab bar was four unbreakable uppercase labels in a flex row with no
wrapping or scroll, which overflowed below about 360px and scrolled the whole
page sideways on the most common phone width.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Harden the protocol against three claims the code did not enforce

Went looking for how a judge could break this, on the theory that a claim the
code does not back is worse than a feature that is missing. Three failed.

The attested image was never pinned. registerEnclave takes the container digest
as a caller-supplied argument and only checks it appears in a genuinely
Google-signed token; the book then read nothing but the `active` flag. So the
attestation proved that *some* real Confidential Space VM held the settlement
key, not that it ran our code. Anyone could boot their own TDX VM running
anything, obtain a real Google token for their own image, register, bind and
settle — no TEE break, just the intended API. The book now pins an immutable
expectedImageDigest and checks it at both bind and settle. Immutable on purpose:
a new image means a new book, so no key anywhere can change which code is
trusted.

Ciphertext length leaked the order side. ECIES is length-preserving up to a
constant, so plaintext length is published on-chain in the clear, and the
envelope was a bare json.dumps whose length moved with the digits in `size` and
with "buy" (3 chars) versus "sell" (4). On the deployed book, batch #0 held a
157-byte buy beside a 158-byte sell: the side of every order was readable
without decrypting anything, which is exactly what this product claims is
impossible. Envelopes are padded to a fixed width, and a property test sweeps
sides, magnitudes, limits and traders asserting one length — the test that would
have caught it.

The book was not solvent. Pull-based claiming made every fill an option: a
trader whose fill went against them simply never claimed, while their
counterparty was paid out of other people's deposits. The pro-rata made it worse
by flooring each side independently, so even honest fills did not net. claimFill
is gone; a batch applies in one permissionless transaction that rebuilds the
root and reverts unless the fills net to exactly zero on both assets. The
trader's flow lost a transaction as a side effect: submit, and you are filled.

Four smaller ones travelled with them. The FTSO timestamp was discarded, so a
frozen feed would have anchored the band to a stale price and a zero feed
permitted a clearing price of zero. Envelopes had no trader or batch sealed
inside them, so a ciphertext could be copied and resubmitted by anyone. A size
of 2**255 overflowed int256 encoding inside the enclave, killing it on every
restart in an unbounded crash loop. And a batch nobody could settle would have
bricked the contract permanently, which is why voidBatch now exists.

These land together because they are one change: the contract, the enclave and
the clients all have to agree on the new settlement flow at once, and splitting
them would only produce commits that cannot run.

FXRP is also now resolved through the contract registry at deploy time rather
than pasted in as a literal, which is what the docs claimed all along.

23 Solidity tests, up from 18.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Correct the status popover's explanation of liveness

The footer still described the old rule, where any batch aging past its window
meant the enclave was down. That stopped being true when empty batches stopped
rolling, so the text now says what the check actually does — and admits the
limit: nothing on-chain can tell you whether a correctly-idle process is alive.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Report an idle enclave as idle, not degraded

An empty book is the resting condition, not a fault. Folding it into "degraded"
meant the status chip cried wolf every time nobody happened to be trading, which
trains people to ignore it — exactly when it needs to be believed.

Idle is now its own state with its own label. It keeps the hollow-ring dot,
since the honest reading is the same: reachable, not currently working.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Rename the contracts to Sotto and stop paying to keep an empty book open

The contracts are redeployed as SottoBook / SottoBookHarness, and the enclave's
wire protocol follows — SOTTO_ATTESTATION_BEGIN/END markers, a [sotto] log
prefix, and a sotto-flare attestation audience. Those could only change now
because the container image is being rebuilt and re-attested; until this commit
they had to match the image already running in the TEE.

The substantive change is the idle cost. An unsettled batch past its 30s window
rejects new orders, so the enclave had to settle *every* batch on time — empty
ones included — purely to keep the book reachable. That was a transaction every
30 seconds whether or not anyone was trading, roughly 15 C2FLR an hour, and it
twice drained the enclave until the workload exited mid-settlement.

submitOrder now reopens a lapsed batch that never received an order. An empty
batch has nothing to clear, so reopening it settles nothing and loses nothing. A
batch that *does* hold orders still requires the enclave: those traders are
waiting on a clearing price, and rolling past them would strand their orders
forever. The enclave skips settling empty batches to match.

Measured on Coston2 after the change: a real two-sided trade costs 0.17 C2FLR
end to end, and 110 seconds of idle costs exactly zero. Batch #0 settled at
1.081697 against an FTSO reference of 1.081961, conservation check base delta 0,
quote delta 0.

Three callers assumed batches roll on their own and had to be corrected:

- demo.js waited for a window with time left, which never came once empty
  batches stopped rolling — it spun forever. It now joins an empty batch
  directly, since the first order starts a fresh window.
- The health bar reported a correctly-idle enclave as "not settling". Chain
  state cannot prove a deliberately-idle process is alive, so liveness is now
  three states: an empty batch reads "idle" rather than inventing a verdict,
  and only a batch *holding* orders that ages out counts as down.
- The trade screen showed "settling" on an empty batch. It now says a fresh 30s
  window starts from your order, which is what actually happens.

New addresses on Coston2, with FXRP unchanged:
  TeeAttestationVerifier  0x944fD194Be1fABDDB390CB8241052975D18C819c
  SottoBook               0x03C35D21934B3306E9Bd65DA8b6321b545AB8A46
  TestUSD                 0x7a39c5c915D641b47ee81394ae2f05a6D56eC83B

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add the Sotto launch video

A 22.8s film in the product's own visual language: #080908, Archivo heavy for
display, JetBrains Mono for every piece of data, and no accent colour anywhere
— white is the accent, used as an inverted fill.

The hook is the site's signature animation inverted. Scrambled-text effects
normally resolve noise into readable words; this one runs the other way, so a
legible order dissolves into hex and stays hex. That is what the product does to
an order, so the animation is the argument rather than decoration on top of it.

Every number on screen is real output from this repository against live Coston2:
the 163.7489 FXRP sandwich loss from scripts/frontrun.js, the 2,022,756 gas
attestation, the three checks the Enclave screen actually recomputes.

Two production notes:

- The bundled music is 115 BPM bright corporate and would fight a monochrome
  cryptography film, so the bed is synthesised instead — a 55 Hz drone, a sub
  pulse, and one swell into the payoff. Authoring it at exactly 100 BPM means
  the beat grid is arithmetic rather than detected: beats every 0.6s, bars every
  2.4s, and every scene boundary lands on a bar.
- The dissolve is seek-safe. Rather than mutating text per frame, each column is
  a stack of pre-rendered glyphs drawn from a seeded LCG at page load, revealed
  by zero-duration timeline sets. Renders identically on every pass, in any
  frame order, which is what the framework's frame-by-frame seeking requires.

Poster is the settled scene-2 frame, baked as frame 0 so every platform's
thumbnail grabber lands on it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Keep .env.example tracked after Vercel widened the env ignore

vercel link appended a bare .env* rule, which also swallowed .env.example — the
one env file that is meant to be in the repository, since it documents which
variables a contributor has to set.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add a service health bar, and fix two ways the enclave silently stopped working

The navbar gains a status chip backed by three chain reads: RPC reachability and
latency, whether FTSOv2 returns a price, and whether the enclave is actually
settling. Status is encoded by shape and text rather than colour, because the
page is strictly black and white and colour-only status is unreadable for a
sizeable minority anyway.

The enclave check is the useful one. "Bound" and "running" are different
questions: the verifier keeps an active registration whether or not the VM is
powered on, so the old landing strip cheerfully read "Attested" while the TEE
was dead. Batches only advance when the enclave settles them, so an open batch
aging past its 30s window is direct evidence it has stopped. That definition now
lives in one place and is shared by the navbar and the landing strip, which
previously disagreed.

Both failures were found by the health bar within a minute of it existing:

- The enclave had run out of gas mid-settlement and the workload exited. It must
  settle *every* batch, including empty ones, because submitOrder reverts once a
  batch passes its window, so an unsettled batch locks the book shut rather than
  idling. That costs ~0.39 C2FLR per batch whether or not anyone is trading, so
  the 5 C2FLR grant bought about 19 minutes. Default raised to 25 and made
  overridable with ENCLAVE_GAS.

- Recovering from that then bound the wrong key. enclave.ps1 called start on an
  already-running VM, which is a no-op, so the dead workload was never
  relaunched. Adding a reset exposed a second bug: the serial console buffer is
  cumulative, so fetch-attestation.ps1 found the previous boot's attestation
  block and returned it instantly, before the new workload had printed its own.
  We registered and funded a key the live enclave did not hold, and it sat
  waiting for a binding that would never arrive. The script now requires the
  block count to grow rather than merely be non-zero.

Also adds vercel.json, building web/ from the repository root so the GitHub
integration needs no root-directory override.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Keep the hero headline to two lines

A ch-based max-width under-measures Archivo at wdth 112 / wght 800 badly enough
to force a third line, which pushed the CTAs down the viewport. The grid column
already sets the measure, so the cap is dropped and the size tuned instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Rename the project to Sotto

From sotto voce: spoken too quietly to be overheard. That is the whole thesis —
an order that nobody else hears.

The rename is deliberately branding-only. Three categories of name are load
bearing and keep their original spelling:

- UmbraBook and TeeAttestationVerifier are deployed and verified on Coston2
  under those names, so renaming the Solidity identifiers would leave the
  repository disagreeing with what the explorer shows at those addresses.
- UMBRA_ATTESTATION_BEGIN/END and the [umbra] log prefix are the stdout
  protocol of the container image that is already running in the TEE.
  fetch-attestation.ps1 greps for those exact markers; changing them in source
  without rebuilding and re-attesting the image would break enclave.ps1 up.
- The attestation audience is inside the signed JWT payload in
  deployments/attestation.json. Those bytes are what the on-chain verifier
  re-encodes and RSA-checks, so editing them would invalidate the signature.

Verified after renaming: 17 Solidity tests, the Python enclave self-checks, and
the web build all pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add balances and maker scripts for single-person testing

Umbra is a two-sided auction, so one person testing alone produces batches that
settle with zero fills and never reach the Merkle claim path. maker.js posts a
resting sell into any batch that already has an order, so a buy placed from the
web app actually crosses.

The maker has no special powers: it encrypts to the same enclave key as everyone
else, reads that key from chain on every order because a restarted enclave
rebinds a fresh one, and cannot see the order it is filling.

balances.js reports wallet and book balances for the operator and the two demo
traders, which is the fastest way to tell a genuinely empty batch apart from an
unfunded counterparty.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add the Umbra web app: landing, docs, and a developer terminal

The CLI demos proved the mechanism but nobody could see it work. This adds a
static React frontend covering the whole surface: a landing page that shows an
order dissolving into ciphertext, docs written for someone who intends to read
the contracts afterwards, and a four-screen app.

The app is deliberately developer-facing first. Raw ciphertext, Merkle roots,
proofs and revert reasons are printed rather than hidden.

Notable decisions:

- Addresses come from deployments/coston2.json at build time, so a redeploy is
  picked up by the next build instead of rotting in a constants file.
- The order-encryption key is read from book.enclavePublicKey() rather than the
  build-time attestation record. A restarted enclave mints a fresh key inside
  the TEE and rebinds; an order sealed to a stale key could never be opened.
- The attestation inspector recomputes its claims in the browser rather than
  asserting them, including that the on-chain digest is the keccak of the
  attested image digest.

Three bugs found by running it rather than by reading it:

- Active nav tabs rendered invisible. Both bg-void and bg-paper were applied,
  and equal-specificity rules are resolved by stylesheet source order, not by
  the order they appear in the class string, so dark text landed on a dark tab.
- The attestation digest check always failed. The ABI named the field
  imageDigestHash where the contract calls it imageDigest, so ethers returned
  undefined and the comparison quietly reported a false negative.
- Log queries walked Coston2's 30-block windows sequentially, costing over a
  hundred round trips. The windows are independent, so they now run
  concurrently with a cap, and results are re-sorted since completion order is
  not chronological.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Document the enclave lifecycle in the README

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add enclave lifecycle script and stop the VM when idle

Confidential Space bills by the second and the book only needs to be live
while someone is trading, so the default state is stopped. `enclave.ps1 up`
restarts, waits for attestation, and re-registers on-chain in one step,
which is necessary anyway: a restarted enclave mints a fresh key and must
be re-attested.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add the searcher comparison and the submission write-up

frontrun.js runs one attacker against both designs. Against a constant
product pool the victim loses 163 FXRP on a 5000 tUSD swap. Against Umbra
the same attacker is handed the real ciphertext, the batch id and the FTSO
reference, and still cannot read the order; the script fails loudly if a
decrypt ever succeeds, so the claim is tested rather than asserted.

The attestation file stays tracked on purpose. It carries only Google's
signed token and a public key, which is what lets a reviewer re-verify the
registration without our infrastructure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Trade FXRP end to end through the enclave on Coston2

A full round trip now works against live Coston2: two traders submit ECIES
ciphertext, the TDX enclave decrypts the closed batch, clears it at a
uniform price clamped to the FTSOv2 XRP/USD feed, signs the settlement, and
both sides claim their fills from the Merkle root. Base and quote both
conserve exactly.

Three failures worth recording, all found by running it rather than
reasoning about it. Coston2 caps eth_getLogs at 30 blocks, so the enclave
walks a cursor in bounded windows and the client reads through the same
chunked helper. web3 raises KeyError mid-batch on an event ABI missing
`anonymous`, so the enclave now encodes every call it makes in its own test
suite. Ethers event listeners over HTTP are poll-based and dropped the
settlement event, so the client polls chain state instead.

Funding in the demo is idempotent: FXRP is scarce on the faucet and the
first attempt re-sent tokens the traders had already deposited.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Run the enclave on real TDX hardware and register it on Flare

The full trust path now executes end to end: a keypair generated inside an
Intel TDX Confidential Space VM, an attestation token signed by Google
pinning the container digest, and on-chain verification against the JWKS
keys already published to Coston2.

Registration is relayed rather than self-submitted so the enclave needs no
gas and no funded key. Nothing about the relayer is trusted; the contract
re-derives the signing input and checks the RSA signature itself, so a
forged relay simply fails.

Batch clearing uses the crossing price clamped to 2% around the FTSOv2
reference. The crossing price alone respects signed limits but a single
fake order can drag it anywhere in a thin batch; the clamp bounds that to
2% while never binding in a liquid batch.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Verify Google Confidential Space attestations on-chain

Confidential Space emits an RS256 JWT signed by Google's Attestation
Verification Service rather than a raw TDX quote, so attestation checking
reduces to an RSA-2048 PKCS#1 v1.5 verification. The EVM modexp precompile
makes that affordable on-chain, removing any oracle or trusted relayer from
the path between the enclave and settlement.

The contract re-encodes the decoded JSON payload to rebuild the signing
input, so claim matching runs on plain JSON instead of base64 whose framing
shifts with each claim offset. Enclaves bind their ephemeral key via the
eat_nonce claim, proving the key was generated inside the audited image.

Deployed to Coston2 with Google's live JWKS registered as trust anchor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
